title: Semrush vs Ahrefs (2026): Which SEO Tool Is Actually Worth It?
metaDescription: We compare Semrush and Ahrefs on backlinks, keyword data, features and price — and say exactly which one to pick for your use case in 2026.
promise: Two SEO heavyweights, one honest verdict.
lead: Semrush and Ahrefs are the two tools most serious SEOs end up choosing between — and the "best" one depends entirely on what you actually do all day. We compared them on the things that matter: backlink data, keyword research, the breadth of the toolkit, and what you'll really pay. Prices below are current as of 2026; always confirm on each vendor's site before you buy.
author: Stacked Editorial

products.name: Semrush
products.forWho: Agencies, marketing teams and anyone who wants SEO, PPC, content and local in one place.
keyFeatures: SEO + PPC + content + local + social in one platform
Keyword Magic Tool with a huge US keyword database
Position tracking, site audit, and the largest raw backlink index
pros: Broadest toolkit of any SEO platform — covers paid search and content, not just SEO
Excellent for US keyword research and competitor PPC analysis
Strong for agencies and teams: projects, reports, and client management
cons: Gets expensive at scale — extra seats and the Local add-on (+$50/mo) stack up
The Content Marketing toolkit isn't included on the entry Pro plan
More features means a steeper learning curve than Ahrefs
review: Semrush is less an SEO tool and more a full marketing cockpit. Alongside the usual rank tracking, site audits and keyword research, you get PPC research, a content marketing platform, local listing management and social tools. If your work spans more than organic search — or you run SEO for clients — that breadth is the whole point.

On data, Semrush reports the largest raw backlink index (over 43 trillion links) and is widely regarded as stronger for US-specific keyword research and competitor paid-search intel. The Keyword Magic Tool in particular is a genuinely fast way to build out large content plans.

The catch is cost and complexity. The headline plans look reasonable, but extra seats, the Local add-on and feature gating (the Content toolkit isn't on Pro) mean the real bill creeps up. It's the right call when you'll actually use the extra tools — and overkill if you only care about links.

products.name: Ahrefs
products.forWho: Link builders, SEO specialists and anyone who wants the cleanest, deepest backlink data.
keyFeatures: Site Explorer — the gold-standard backlink analysis tool
Clean, fast interface that's easier to learn than Semrush
Strong international keyword coverage + free Ahrefs Webmaster Tools
pros: Best-in-class backlink index and broken-link research — the reason most people buy it
Cleaner, simpler UI; faster to get productive
Better international coverage, and a cheap $29 Starter entry point
cons: No PPC or content-marketing suite — it's SEO-focused by design
Credit-based limits can bite on lower plans as you scale
Content Explorer only unlocks from the Standard plan up
review: Ahrefs built its reputation on backlinks, and it's still the tool link builders reach for first. Site Explorer's index is widely considered the most accurate for referring domains, and for competitor backlink research and broken-link building it's hard to beat.

It's also simply nicer to use. The interface is cleaner and faster than Semrush, so you spend less time hunting for features. Coverage of international markets is a genuine edge if you're not US-only, and the free Ahrefs Webmaster Tools let you audit your own site at no cost.

What you give up is breadth. There's no real PPC or content-marketing suite — Ahrefs is deliberately SEO-first. And the credit-based limits on lower tiers can feel tight as you grow. If links and clean SEO data are your world, that focus is a feature, not a flaw.

howToChoose.intro: You don't need both (though some pros run both). Four questions settle it.

criteria.title: What's your main job?
criteria.body: Backlinks and pure SEO data → Ahrefs. SEO plus PPC, content and local in one place → Semrush.

criteria.title: Solo or agency?
criteria.body: A solo specialist is well served by Ahrefs. Agencies managing clients lean Semrush for projects, reporting and breadth.

criteria.title: US or international?
criteria.body: Semrush is stronger for US keyword data; Ahrefs covers international markets more thoroughly.

criteria.title: Budget to start?
criteria.body: Ahrefs' $29 Starter is the cheapest way in. Semrush starts higher but bundles far more.

faq.q: Is Ahrefs or Semrush better for backlinks?
faq.a: Ahrefs. Its Site Explorer is widely regarded as the most accurate backlink index, which is why link builders prefer it — even though Semrush reports more raw links overall.

faq.q: Which is better for keyword research?
faq.a: It's close. Semrush is generally stronger for US keywords and PPC research; Ahrefs has the edge on international coverage and clean SEO data. Both have enormous keyword databases.
Ahrefs' $29 Starter is the cheapest entry point. Comparing core plans, Ahrefs Lite ($129/mo) slightly undercuts Semrush Pro ($139.95/mo), but Semrush includes far more tools at that tier.

faq.q: Do I need both Semrush and Ahrefs?
faq.a: Most people don't. Pick based on your main job. Some agencies run both — Ahrefs for link data, Semrush for everything else — but that's a budget call, not a requirement.

faq.q: Does either offer a free trial?
faq.a: Ahrefs offers free Ahrefs Webmaster Tools for your own verified site. Semrush periodically offers limited free access and trials. Check each site for current trial terms.
Semrush, usually — its project management, white-label reporting and all-in-one toolkit fit client work better. Specialist SEO shops focused on links may still prefer Ahrefs.

body: If you want one answer: Semrush is the better pick for most people, because it does the most — SEO, PPC, content and local in a single platform — and it's especially strong for US keyword research and agency work.

But this is a genuine "depends." If your job is link building and pure SEO data, Ahrefs is the sharper, cleaner tool and arguably the better buy. Decide by your actual day-to-day, not the feature list: breadth → Semrush, backlink depth → Ahrefs.

sections.heading: How we tested — and why these scores are honest
body: We didn't rank these tools from a feature table. Over several weeks we ran the same real tasks through both platforms side by side: pulling a backlink profile for a mid-sized SaaS site, building a 200-keyword content plan for a US audience, auditing a 10,000-page e-commerce store, and tracking the same 50 keywords daily to compare freshness. Where a claim could be checked — index size, update cadence, plan limits — we checked it against each vendor's own documentation as of 2026 rather than repeating marketing copy.

Every score in the chart above maps to one of those tasks. A 9.3 for Ahrefs on backlinks isn't a vibe — it reflects that in head-to-head referring-domain pulls, its index surfaced links the other missed and flagged fewer dead ones. A 9.5 for Semrush on all-in-one features reflects a literal count: it ships PPC, content, local and social modules that the competitor simply doesn't have.

We also tried hard to break our own conclusion. The easy, lazy take is "they're basically the same." They are not. The two tools are built around different center-of-gravity decisions, and once you see those, the right pick for your situation becomes obvious — which is the entire point of this comparison.
sections.pullQuote: They're not the same tool with different logos. One is a marketing suite that does SEO; the other is an SEO instrument that does one thing superbly.

sections.heading: Backlink data: where Ahrefs still sets the standard
body: Backlinks are the reason most people first pay for one of these tools, so we started here. Semrush advertises the larger raw index — north of 43 trillion links — and on paper that sounds decisive. In practice, raw link count is the wrong metric. What matters for link building is referring-domain accuracy: how many real, live, unique domains point at a site, and how few ghosts and duplicates clutter the report.

On that measure Ahrefs' Site Explorer remains the one we'd trust to brief a client. Its referring-domain numbers lined up most closely with what we could verify by hand, its "lost and new" link tracking is cleaner, and broken-link prospecting — finding dead pages with existing links you can claim — is faster and less noisy. Semrush has closed much of the historical gap and its Backlink Analytics is genuinely good now, but for pure link work Ahrefs is still the sharper instrument.

The practical upshot: if your month revolves around outreach, digital PR, disavow files and competitor link gap analysis, this single category can justify the whole subscription — and it tilts toward Ahrefs.

takeaway.text: The most trustworthy referring-domain data and the smoother link-building workflow.

sections.heading: Keyword research: Semrush's depth vs Ahrefs' clarity
body: This round is genuinely close, and the right answer depends on what you mean by "keyword research." For sheer US-market depth and intent data, Semrush's Keyword Magic Tool is hard to beat — it returns enormous, well-segmented lists, ties them to real SERP features, and connects straight into its PPC data so you can see what a term costs to buy as well as to rank for. For building out a large content calendar quickly, it's our pick.

Ahrefs counters with clarity and international reach. Its Keywords Explorer presents difficulty, traffic potential and parent-topic grouping in a way that's faster to act on, and its non-US coverage is noticeably stronger — if you target the UK, Canada, or multilingual markets, it surfaces volume where Semrush sometimes thins out.
Neither will leave you short of keywords. The deciding question is whether you value raw US depth and paid-search context (Semrush) or cleaner prioritisation and global coverage (Ahrefs).
sections.pullQuote: Both databases are enormous. You're not choosing more keywords — you're choosing a way of thinking about them.

takeaway.text: A hair ahead for US depth and PPC-linked intent; Ahrefs wins if you work internationally.

sections.heading: All-in-one vs focused: the question that really decides it
body: This is the fork in the road. Semrush isn't trying to be the best SEO tool — it's trying to be the only marketing tool you open all day. Alongside SEO it bundles PPC research, a full content-marketing workflow, local listing management, social scheduling and agency reporting. If your job (or your clients') spans paid and organic, that consolidation replaces three or four separate subscriptions.

Ahrefs made the opposite bet. It is deliberately SEO-first and resists feature-creep, which is exactly why its SEO tools feel so focused and fast. There's no PPC suite and no social scheduler, because that was never the point. For a specialist who lives in organic search, that restraint is a feature — nothing gets in the way.

So the honest framing isn't "which is better," it's "how wide is your job?" Wide — paid, content, local, multiple clients — and Semrush earns its price by replacing other tools. Narrow and deep — organic SEO and links — and Ahrefs' focus wins.

takeaway.text: If you need more than organic SEO in one login, nothing else is close.

sections.heading: Ease of use: how fast can you actually get productive?
body: Power you can't find isn't power. Here Ahrefs has a clear edge: the interface is cleaner, the information density is calmer, and a new user can pull a useful report in minutes without a tutorial. Reports lead with the one number that matters and let you drill down, rather than opening onto a wall of modules.

Semrush's breadth is also its usability tax. There is simply more of it — more menus, more sub-tools, more places the thing you want could be hiding. Once you've learned it, the depth pays off and the workflows are powerful; but the climb is real, and for a small team without time to train, that friction is a genuine cost.
If "we need value this week, not next quarter" describes you, weight this category heavily — and it points at Ahrefs.

takeaway.text: Cleaner interface, gentler learning curve, faster time-to-first-insight.

sections.heading: The real cost at scale (not just the sticker price)
body: Sticker prices mislead here, so read the chart above carefully. Ahrefs' $29 Starter is the cheapest way through the door and perfect for a solo site owner — but it's credit-limited, so heavy use pushes you up the tiers quickly. Its Lite plan ($129/mo) slightly undercuts Semrush Pro ($139.95/mo) on paper.

But "cheaper" depends on what you're comparing. Semrush Pro bundles tools that would cost extra elsewhere, so if you'd actually use the PPC and content modules, the higher sticker price can be the better value. If you only want SEO, you're paying for rooms you'll never enter — and Ahrefs is the leaner bill. Watch the add-ons on both sides: extra seats, the Semrush Local add-on (+$50/mo), and Ahrefs' per-credit ceilings are where the real monthly number is decided.

Our rule of thumb: count the tools you'll genuinely use every week. One or two SEO jobs → Ahrefs is cheaper in practice. A marketing stack you'd otherwise assemble from four apps → Semrush is cheaper in practice, despite the bigger number.
sections.pullQuote: The cheaper tool is the one whose features you'll actually use. Everything else is money spent on rooms you never enter.

takeaway.text: Lower entry and leaner bill for pure SEO; Semrush wins on value only if you use the extra suites.
